quote: equal to 329 metres or 1079.12 English feet…4.88 U to the mile—in round numbers say 5
finding: Mirchandani takes the li after Gaubil as 329 m, i.e. 4.88 li to the English mile (about 5), and uses 4.88 throughout his distance reckonings.

topic: value of the li; against Cunningham
quote: allows 6 li to the mile as a practical road-measure, but that valuation of the li does not give consistent results
finding: He rejects Cunningham's 6 li to the mile as inconsistent.

topic: method: capital to capital, Records over Life
quote: almost always the distances and directions from one capital to the next one described by him…and these I have neither modified nor disregarded to suit my identifications
finding: He reads every bearing and distance as capital-to-capital and prefers the Records to the Life where they differ.

topic: country = Vṛṣadarbha west of the Indus (Derajat), not Sind
quote: It was this kingdom of Vr^darbha that was visited by the pilgrim…Sindhu was evidently its popular name, derived from the river Indus
finding: He identifies Sin-tu with the Puranic kingdom of Vṛṣadarbha on the west bank of the Indus in the Derajat (Dera Ghazi Khan), distinct from the Sind of the Chachnama, and calls 'Sindhu' only its popular name.

topic: name Sindh in Dera Ghazi Khan
quote: the level portion of Dera Ghazi Khan District…the present day called Sindh after the river Indus
finding: In support he cites the gazetteer: the riverine strip of Dera Ghazi Khan District is still called Sindh.

topic: rock salt → Salt Range in Sin-tu
quote: Salt Bange was included, in whole or in part, in the Sin-tu kingdom
finding: He argues that the white rock salt means the Salt Range belonged to Sin-tu, since rock salt is found nowhere lower down the Indus.

quote: The real name of the city, as conjectured by me from Sanskrit literary sources, was VTsadarhha-pura
finding: He restores 毘苫婆補羅 as Vṛṣadarbhapura, named after Śibi's son Vṛṣadarbha (Pargiter), against Julien's Vijambhapura.

topic: capital site: S Dera Ghazi Khan, near Mithankot
quote: Vrs&darbha-pura was situated in the south of the present Dera Ghazi Khan District, somewhere below the point of confluence of
finding: He places the capital, now untraced, in southern Dera Ghazi Khan District on the west bank of the Indus below the Panjnad confluence, near Mithankot. He gives no exact site.

quote: Mithankot, situated not many miles south of the point where the Panjnad joins the Indus is distant about 300 miles as the crow flies from B hinmal
finding: 1900 li (c. 380 miles) north from Bhinmal, then crossing the Indus to the west, brings him to southern Dera Ghazi Khan, c. 300 miles straight-line from Bhinmal.

quote: was 700 li, or 140 miles, east of the capital of
finding: He says the Life's 700 li east of 'O-fan-ch'a (Gandava) also fits a capital in southern Dera Ghazi Khan.

topic: against Alor / Sind (Cunningham, Haig, Watters, Smith, Lambrick)
quote: that Pi-shen-p*o-pu-lo was perhaps another name or…are entirely unwarranted
finding: He rejects the attempts by Cunningham, Watters, Smith, Vaidya and Lambrick to fit Sin-tu to the Sind of Chach: a 'book-name' for Alor, a Śūdra Rai king in 641, and an error in Multan's bearing. Haig had already found the two accounts irreconcilable.

quote: Hiuen Tseng’s Sindh, in fact, is not the Sindh of any period known to history
finding: He quotes Haig: the capital is put west of the Indus, Multan only 900 li to the east, and the king a Śūdra where the Chachnama has a Brahman ruling c. 641.

quote: Banfill identified this capital with Vijnot…Vijnot, however, does not fit the position assigned to the capital by Hiuen
finding: He rejects Banfill's Vijnot in Upper Sind (and Anderson's Bheekumpoor in Bikaner).

quote: the fact remains that he did not visit the Lower Indus valley
finding: On his reading Xuanzang never entered Sind proper. 'O-tien-p'o-chi-lo, Pi-to-shi-lo and 'O-fan-ch'a are all in Baluchistan, not Sind.

topic: Multan; Sin-tu and Multan on opposite banks
quote: Sin-tu and Multan, thus, according to Hiuen Tsiang, were neighbouring kingdoms in the Punjab, lying on the opposite sides of the Indus
finding: He accepts Mūlasthānapura = Multan and puts Sin-tu across the Indus from it in the Punjab.

quote: represents the length of his journey in two directions, first east and then north
finding: He takes the 900 li as a route first east across the Indus and then north along its east bank, with detours in marshy country. He calls Watters' summary (capital 900 li west of Multan) misleading.

quote: Watters (ii, p. 254) is needlessly doubtful about this identification
finding: He defends the restoration Mūlasthānapura against Watters, citing the sun temple with its golden image, which also appears in the Chachnama and the Arab geographers.

quote: Pi-lo-mo-lo has been erroneously identified by Cunningham with modem Banner
finding: He takes 毘羅摩羅 as Bhillamāla = Bhinmal, the Gurjara capital of the 6th–9th centuries, against Cunningham's Barmer, which he says was founded only in the 13th century.

quote: This statement is, of course, a mistake, for that bearing from Suratha
finding: He dismisses the Life's statement that Xuanzang went west from Surāṣṭra (Kathiawar) to 'O-tien-p'o-chi-lo: that bearing would put the country in the sea.

topic: route: 1500–1600 li SW from Sin-tu, via Kachhi
quote: D^jat via Kachhi or Kachh Gaftd&va region of Baluchistan
finding: He has Xuanzang go 1500–1600 li south-west from the Derajat to Las Bela through Kachhi, avoiding Sind.

quote: describes as a Buddhist principality subject to the kingdom of Sind, on the high road to Makran
finding: He identifies 'O-tien-p'o-chi-lo with the Armabel of the Chachnama, a Buddhist principality subject to Sind on the road to Makran, i.e. the Las Bela State.

quote: there is no reason to doubt that Armabel corresponds with…which is now represented by the Las Bela State
finding: He holds that Las Bela fits both the position (sea to the south, Makran to the west) and the description: saline low ground, scrub and herds. He extends it east to the Indus.

quote: was ruled by a Buddhist chief, who “had revolted from his allegiance”
finding: He cites the Chachnama's Buddhist ruler of Armabel in 631, who submitted to Chach, to match Xuanzang's 80 monasteries and a country 'subject to Sind' without a ruler of its own.

topic: Armabel does not match the transcription
quote: Armdhel does not sufficiently accord with cither
finding: He admits that Armabel, the Arabic name, does not match the Chinese transcription phonetically.

quote: The general direction of Cutch from…is south, not south-west…Cutch is neither bounded by Makran on ihe west nor by the Indus on the east
finding: Against Cunningham's Cutch and Koteśvara (with Sykes and Haig): Cutch lies south, not south-west, of Sin-tu. It borders neither Makran nor the Indus, reaching it would need an unmentioned crossing of the Indus, and the name does not transcribe Cutch.

topic: against Haig's Maheśvara temple at Koteshwar
quote: bear out the statement of Haig about the presence of a temple of Mahesvara at Koteswar
finding: He notes that the Cutch Gazetteer does not support Haig's claim of a Maheśvara temple at Koteshwar.

quote: it is quite certain that the port of Debal was not included in it
finding: He rejects Smith's and Lambrick's Indus Delta and Lambrick's capital at Debal. The Chachnama has Debal governed for Chach by his brother in 636, so it was not part of 'O-tien-p'o-chi-lo.

quote: I have no doubt these ruins occupy the site of the ancient city of Khie-tsi-shi-fa-lo
finding: He places 朅䶩濕伐羅 at the ruins of Gondakahar, 11 miles NW of Bela, with Buddhist caves at Gondrani nearby. He suggests it is also the Rambakia of Alexander's historians.

topic: capital fixed from 700 li N to Kusdar
quote: 700 li, or 143 miles (at 4.88 li to the mile), north from Khie-tsi-shi-far-lo…Kusdar, which lies 139 miles north from modem Bela
finding: He fixes the capital by counting back 700 li (143 miles) south from Kusdar, the capital of Pi-to-shi-lo, which lies 139 miles north of Bela.

quote: fied this capital with modern Karachi, but the identification is, no doubt, a mistaken one
finding: He rejects Vivien de Saint-Martin's (and Sykes') Karachi, and Khaira Kot 33 miles south of Bela because it is too far from Kusdar. He leaves the name's Sanskrit form open apart from -īśvara.

quote: about 400 miles (“less than 2000 li”)
finding: He measures the 2000 li westward from Gondakahar as nearly 400 miles along the Kech valley.

quote: Greater Makran, I should think, would be quite an appropriate modem designation for this country
finding: He takes Long-kie-lo to be Makran, Baluchi and Persian together, with parts of Kharan and Jhalawan.

quote: could only have been the valley of Kech that traverses Makran from east to west
finding: He identifies Xuanzang's 'long valley' with the Kech (Kej) valley, the natural highway from Las Bela to Persia. He uses this, with medieval reports of Makran's fertility, to fit the 'dense population'.

quote: It is the only likely place in Persian Makian with which the capital of Long-kie-lo can properly be identified
finding: He identifies 窣菟黎濕伐羅 with Kasarkand in Persian Makran. Bela to Gayab at the west end of the Kech valley is 308 miles, and Kasarkand lies c. 75 miles further west. Geh and Bint are too far.

quote: situated near the western extremity of the Kech valley, the distance is 308 miles
finding: He uses the gazetteer route distance Bela–Gayab (308 miles) to bring the 400 miles out to Kasarkand.

quote: when Hiuen Tsiang visited the country in A.D. 641 he found it
finding: He reconciles 'under the government of Persia' with the Chachnama: Makran passed between Sind and Persia, Chach absorbed it c. 631, and it was again under Persia by 641.

quote: the possible equivalents are Rahgala, Lahgara, Langala…I confess the Chinese designation, which I am thus unable to elucidate
finding: He leaves 狼揭羅 unexplained. Petech reads it as *lang g'lat la (Raṅgala, Laṅgara, Laṅgala) and rules out a corruption of Lang for Makara. He does not propose Sthūleśvara here; that comes in his 1969 paper.

quote: This identification has nothing to support it except some similarity of sound between Lakura and lAnkara
finding: He rejects Cunningham's capital at Lākoriān/Lakura between Khozdar and Kalat (bearing changed to north-west) and his 'Baluchistan', siding with Watters' dismissal.

quote: included the modern Las Bela, together probably with parts of Jhalawan and Eastern Makran
finding: He notes Lambrick's Las Bela–Jhalawan–E Makran (which follows from Lambrick's delta for 11.18) and Anderson's and Majumdar's Makran-plus-Kirman. Against the latter he argues from the Chachnama that Kirman was a separate province.

quote: on the north-western frontier o£ which lay the kingdom of Persia
finding: He takes Persia (Po-la-sse) as bordering Long-kie-lo to the north-west and does not discuss it further.

topic: route: back to Las Bela, then 700 li N
quote: From Long-kie-lo Hiuen Tsiang returned to ‘O-tien-p’o-chi-lo
finding: He has Xuanzang return from Makran to Las Bela and go 700 li north. He calls the Life's 700 li NE directly from Long-kie-lo an error.

quote: appear to be the districts of Turan and Budha
finding: He identifies Pi-to-shi-lo with the Arab geographers' and Chachnama's Turān, whose capital was Kusdar, i.e. modern Jhalawan.

quote: be no doubt that Kusdar corresponds to the Chinese
finding: He places the unnamed capital at Kusdar (Khuzdar), 700 li = 143 miles north of Gondakahar.

quote: has reference probably to this Dravidian dialect
finding: He finds Jhalawan's size (21,128 sq mi) and cold winds a fit, and takes the language 'slightly different from Mid-India' to be Brahui. He calls the 'dense population' an exaggeration.

topic: Aśoka stūpa = Masson's mound N of Khuzdar
quote: was probably the remains of the Buddhist monuments
finding: He takes the large mound with burnt brick that Masson saw north of Khuzdar to be the Aśokan stūpa 'about 3 miles north of the capital'.

quote: Pi-to-shi-lo was probably intended as a transcription of
finding: He restores the name as Paṭṭa-śilā, 'rock where four roads meet', for the rocky plain of Kusdar where caravan routes converge. He records Julien's Pītaśilā, Cunningham's Pātaśilā and Watters' Bhedaśira.

quote: rendered it as Pdta-sila or “flat rock” and identified it with Lower Sind, the chief town in which is Hyderabad
finding: He rejects Cunningham's Lower Sind with Hyderabad (Patala), which is the basis of the study's current identification.

quote: was round about Sehwan, or possibly west of the Khirthar range in Jhalawan
finding: He rejects Haig's Nagar Parkar/Umarkot, Anderson's Bukkur and Sykes' Upper Sind route. He notes that Lambrick's second choice (west of the Khirthar, in Jhalawan) matches his own, and that Lambrick's 'not mountainous' objection does not decide the matter.

quote: Kachh Gandava is thus the modern renresentative of the Chinese pilgrim’s country of
finding: He identifies 'O-fan-ch'a with Budha/Budhiya of the Chachnama and Arab geographers, i.e. Kachhi (Kachh Gandava). Elliot notes a place still called Budha on the Nari.

quote: marched from Armabel (Las Bela) via Tiiran to Kandabil
finding: He cites Chach's march from Armabel through Turan to Kandabil as matching Xuanzang's sequence of 11.18, 11.21 and 11.22.

topic: capital = Kandabil = Gandava; 300 li emended to 500
quote: the unnamed capital of *0-fan-ch’a was this city of Kandabil, that is to say, modem Gandava…the figure “300” in the Chinese text is an error for “500”
finding: He places the capital at Kandabil = Gandava, c. 100 miles NE of Kusdar. Since the text gives 300 li (61 miles), he emends 300 to 500.

quote: We would, therefore, be not far wrong in taking the distance between the two capital cities to be 500 li
finding: He cites the gazetteer distances Kusdar–Kotra 84–90 miles plus 8 miles to Gandava, and Bellew's 93 miles via the Mula pass.

quote: The capital of this ancient Buddha, or Ruddhiva kingdom, I believe to b" Armabel
finding: He follows Elliot's Kandabil = Gandava against Raverty, who says Kandabil stood on a hill, and Holdich, who puts the capital at Armabel. He reads the Chachnama's 'Kandahar' as a corruption of Gandava.

quote: the Chach-Ndma expressly states that when Chach, early in his reign, marched from Alor to Budhiya its capital was ICakaraj
finding: He notes a second Hindu-period capital of Budhiya, Kakaraj, 'called Siwis' = Sibi, 70 miles NE of Gandava.

quote: It is no wonder that Hiuen Tsiang found the monks in the place wearing shoes and padded garments
finding: He matches Kachhi's area (5,310 sq mi), wheat on the irrigated west side and the cold north wind at Gandava with Xuanzang's description and the shoes-and-padded-robes legend. He also notes the Dallu Rai mounds near Gajan, 3 miles NE of Gandava.

topic: country = Bolan / Loralai; capital at Duki
quote: I would place the unnamed capital of Fa-la-na at or near that place…included a considerable part of Loralai District and the adjacent tract to the west, together probably with the Bolan Pass
finding: He puts the capital of 伐剌拏 at or near Duki (Loralai District) on the India–Kandahar caravan route, with the country covering Loralai and the Bolan Pass.

topic: distances 180 miles NE of Gandava, 400 miles SE of Ghazni
quote: has to be looked for some 180 miles to the north-east of Gandava and about 400 miles to the south-east of Ghazni
finding: He fixes Fa-la-na at about 180 miles NE of Gandava (900 li) and about 400 miles SE of Ghazni (2000 li). Duki is 125 miles straight-line from Gandava, c. 180 by road.

topic: against Bannu (Cunningham, Stein) and Vaneh (Vivien, Smith, Lambrick)
quote: From Gandava either to Vaenh or to Bannu the distance is a great deal more than 180 miles
finding: He rejects Bannu (Cunningham, Stein) and Vaneh on the Gomal (Vivien, Smith, Lambrick) because both are too far from Gandava and too near Ghazni for the stated distances. This argument depends on putting 'O-fan-ch'a at Gandava.

quote: It is not improbable that the country of Fa-la-na derived its name from this important pass
finding: He derives Fa-la-na from the Bolan Pass (Skt. *Bhalāna; Ṛgvedic Bhalānas), following Anderson 1847.

quote: I am inclined to place it in the Quetta-Pishin region
finding: He identifies 稽疆那 with Kīkānān of the Chachnama and Arab authors and places it in Quetta-Pishin, west of his Fa-la-na. He notes that Cunningham also suggested Pishin-Quetta.

topic: against Stein, Lambrick, Le Strange, Imp. Gaz., Hodivala
quote: Aurel Stein located it in the hill region of Waziristan
finding: He lists and passes over Stein's Waziristan (the study's current view), Lambrick's Loralai–Zhob, Le Strange's Kalat, the Imperial Gazetteer's Nal and Hodivala's Lakoriān.

quote: is without doubt the Kikanan of the Chach-Ncvia and the Arab authors
finding: He cites the Chachnama's north-west boundary of Sind at the mountains of Kusdar and Kīkānān and its horses, matching Xuanzang's fine horses.

quote: is without doubt the Arachosia of the classical writers and Zabul or Zabulistan of the Arab authors
finding: He accepts 漕矩吒 = Arachosia/Zābulistān with 鶴悉那 = Ghazni, reached 2000 li (400 miles) from Fa-la-na.
